full_judgment:
“It’s finding and recommendations are bad in law and any order of the Authority based on such findings and recommendations is also bad in law and cannot be sustained". Reliance was placed on the decision in Amir Hossain's case P.L.D. 1963 (SC) 185. The learned Judge took pain to consider the report of the Screening Committee and the adverse remark in the annual confidential report of the plaintiff and then concluded that such adverse remarks had not been sub-satiated by any specific instances nor such remarks were ever communicated to him and he had no opportunity to represent against them. The learned Judges then came to the conclusion that under section 10 of the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance. 1959, though the order of finding by an appointing authority or Screening Committee cannot be called in Question but the ruling in Zafrul Ahmed's case. 12 DLR (SC) 9 will be attracted and such finding by such authority is therefore not immune from challenge. The learned Judges distinguished the decision in 21 DLR (SC) 16 and 25 DLR (SC) 94 on the ground .that those are the decisions which-rest on the charge of "inefficiency" but in the present case the charge was for 'misconduct'. In this view of the matter the appeal was dismissed. 

 5. Leave was granted to consider the question whether the Learned Judges of the High Court Division were well founded in applying the case of Amir Hossain and whether the principle of Muzuqullah's case and Nasiruddin Ahmed's case are attracted and whether under Article 6(5) (b) of the Laws (Continuance in Force) Order. 1959 the impugned order is immune from challenge. 

 6. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Additional Attorney General in painstaking manner presented the factual aspects of the case and the relevant law. The learned Additional Attorney General submitted that the High Court Division had fallen into an error of taking notice of the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, (1959) (Ordinance III of 1959) and have failed to notice the ratio laid down in two cases (1969) 21 DLR(SC) and (1973) 25 DLR (SC). 

 7. It is unfortunate that the High Court Division considered the provision of the Ordinance III of 1959. That Ordinance was provided for the constitution, power and procedure of the Committee appointed to scrutinise the conduct of certain persons, That Ordinance has given the power to appoint Committee and for recording finding and the procedure of that Committee and then section 10 bars the jurisdiction of the Court. That Ordinance was promulgated on 21st January, 1959 Action was taken in this case under Article 6(51 (b) of the Laws (Continuance in Force Order, 1959. President's Order No. 1 of 1959 dated 9th March, 1959 was promulgated adding new clauses 3 and 4 and clause 5 was subsequently amended by President's Order No. 5 of 1959 promulgated on 23rd April. 1959. The two sub-clauses (a) and (b) of clause 5 of Article 6 as amended are reproduced below: 

 (a) suspended reduced in rank, removed or dismissed for being corrupt or for misconduct or for inefficiency after such enquiry as may be held under the orders of the Central Government; or 

 8. It will be noticed that sub-clause (b) by reference to clause (a) includes "misconduct" as a ground for compulsory retirement of a person in the service, if the order of termination is made before the 1st July, 1959. This provision is a part of a supra constitutional law (Continuance in Force) Order, 1959. It is independent of any other law and has an overriding effect as its says: "nothing in this article or in any law, rule or instrument having force of law shall prevent" a person mentioned in clause (1) from being compulsorily retired under sub-clause (b) and no appeal has been provided for. Since the action against the plaintiff was taken under this provision we fail to understand the reasoning’s of the High Court Division as to how provisions of Ordinance III of 1959 are attracted. As has been noticed in the case Murzuqullah, (1969) 21 DLR (SC) 16, even if any enquiry was made that was merely gratuitous because clause (a) speaks of "after such enquiry as may be held", clause (b) which stands on a different footing' provides for compulsory retirement "for any cause mentioned in (a)" but no enquiry has been provided for taking any action under clause (b). The compulsory retirement order was passed on 3.6.59 and the requirement of Article 6 is that such order must be passed before 1st of July, 1959 and since the Order was passed within the period, i.e. fell within the ambit of the statute and protected by the preclusion clause "no appeal shall lie against such order nor shall such order be called in question in any court". The learned Judges relied on the case of Amir Hossain reported in P.L.D. 1963 (SC)185. In that case enquiry was initiated under the provisions of Ordinance No. III of 1959 and the Screening Committee in a cryptic order recommended removal which reads as under: 

 "Seen explanation Heard in person His prosecution under section 193/468 B.P.C. has been sanctioned by the D.I.I. May be removed for misconduct". 

 9. Mere initiation of a criminal case had weighed with the Screening Committee notwithstanding that the petitioner in that case was tried and acquitted by the Special Judge the Supreme Court considered that in the absence of any finding of guilt, the appointing authority is not in a position to come to such conclusion, since the enquiry on which the screening Committee found the officer guilty is insufficient to sustain it. The bar under section 10 of the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1959 could not be raised because the Supreme Court found "the finding in this case is no finding for which protection against judicial examination can be claimed and the order which proceeded thereon is equally liable to interference". This decision has no manner of application in the present case and the reliance by the High Court Division on this decision was totally irrelevant. In the case of Nazlruddin Ahmed reported in 25 DLR (SC) 94 it was held that there was no bar for the Governor to refer the case of a public servant to the Screening Committee for the assessment of public servant's conduct and for recommendation with reference to any independent enquiry under any particular law and hence the Governor was within his province in ordering retirement of the appellant under sub-clause (b) of Clause (5). It was observed: 

 "The Screening Committee held the enquiry in this case at the request of the Governor; who could indisputably get himself informed as to the truth or otherwise of the allegation against the plaintiff through any agency he must choose in the absence of a provision to the contrary. With respect, we are of the opinion that no question of lack of jurisdiction is invoked in the instant case, either of the Screening Committee to enquire into the allegation against the plaintiff-or the Governor in passing the impugned order of retirement." 

 10. The learned Judges of the High Court Division proceeded on the assumption that the Screening Committee had jurisdiction to hold enquiry into .a charge of misconduct under the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1959 and concluded that "it was therefore a statutory enquiry. Being a statutory enquiry the Screening Committee was bound to hold enquiry in accordance with law". Herein liesthe error. In the present proceeding no enquiry was necessary by any Committee since the Governor could "indisputably get himself informed as to the truth or otherwise of the allegation against the plaintiff' through any agency he might choose in the absence of a provision to the contrary" (Vide 25 D.L.R. S.C. 94). That was the error committed by the trial court and the High Court in 21 D.L.R. (S.C.) 16. The Supreme Court observed: 

 "We regret to say that both the trial Judge and the High Court have gone off the mark in seeking guidance from the provisions of the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1959 and the rules made thereunder, as they were wholly irrelevant in the decision of this case. The High Court in particular had itself pertinently posed the questions whether the officer could be retired compulsorily on the ground of inefficiency under the powers quoted in the impugned order. Yet, while reaching its conclusion it totally lost sight of the nature and extent of that power. The source of the power for retiring the respondent compulsorily, as quoted in the Governor's order, cited above is sub-clause (b) of clause (5) of Article 6 of the Laws (Continuance in Force) Order, 1959". 

 This was the error in the present case also. The decision of Amir Hossain which was decided under Public Conduct Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1959 has no manner of application. The contention of the plaintiff is therefore devoid of any substance and is covered by the two decisions referred to above. The High Court had fallen into error and therefore the order and judgment of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside.
